prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength enable timekeeping and tests of fundamental physics at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a new measurement capability in the strict sense. It joins the statistics of thousands of atoms to the Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of trapped ones, and it has taken fractional uncertainty and instability to the 10^-18 level. Independent Sr and Yb clocks at several institutes agree when compared, which for an instrument is the right standard of reproducibility. Those comparisons are already used for relativistic geodesy at the centimetre to millimetre scale, for limits on drifts of fundamental constants and for dark-matter searches, and the planned redefinition of the second rests on this clock family. The attribution is also unusually clean for this list. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength condition and demonstrated the first lattice clock, and Ye's group brought the platform to record accuracy and stability and into applications, so two names cover the achievement. I weight methods that change what can be observed, and the evidence here is experimental, quantitative and widely reproduced.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an instrument and metrology achievement, and several colleagues (Lindroth explicitly) read it as a technical advance rather than a discovery of new physics. It also builds on prior prizes, the frequency comb (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and the ion-trap and laser-cooling work, and ion clocks and the Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom generation of experiments are not credited. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so the impact case is partly prospective. Finally, B013 has far broader support in this committee (seven top-three placements against my single first place for B006), and I ranked it only eighth because it is outside my field. That low rank reflects my limited ability to judge it, not a considered judgement that it is weak.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B006 sixth and says it is more a technical achievement than a new discovery, while placing atom interferometry (B022) second for its direct demonstration of matter-wave coherence.
responses.response: I partly agree with the framing, and I think it cuts the other way for the discovery-versus-technique line. Both B006 and B022 are measurement-first, so if that distinction is applied consistently it penalises both, and I cannot support B022 on those grounds while setting B006 aside. On substance, the clocks already deliver what the interferometers still promise. Lattice clocks are compared at 10^-18 between independent laboratories and are used for geodesy and constants tests today. Large-baseline atom interferometers for equivalence-principle and gravitational-wave tests are still under construction. I do agree with her on attribution in B022, since Chu, Mlynek and others are spread across the strands, and that is why I keep B022 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B013) first as a genuinely new state of matter, with first-principles band theory and ARPES and transport in quantitative agreement, and notes that recognition is arguably overdue. He would credit Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan and leave Mele out.
responses.response: I take his point on theory-experiment closure, which is the criterion I care about too, and it moves me to rank B013 as my first alternative. I am not persuaded that leaving Mele out is defensible. Kane and Mele together introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal, and Eriksson's own text concedes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe prediction is outside the credited names. Dropping a theorist to fit Hasan's 3D work in a three-person limit penalises the original proposal. The Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio proposed by Danielsson, Mehlig and Olsson seems the cleaner allocation. The allocation problem there is more severe than the one in B006, which makes me hesitate to put the broadest-support candidate ahead of a cleanly attributable one.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube (B008) first because a new observational window is what he values most, but acknowledges that only Halzen is credited and that a fair prize may need people who are not in the supplied credit.
responses.response: I share his criterion, a new window on nature, and that is why I weight B006 so heavily. My difficulty with B008 is exactly the attribution he raises. A prize built on a single credited name for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES precursors and the detector builders omitted, is not something I can assess as fair from this credit list. I also want to know the evidence at the level of reproducibility. The diffuse flux is seen in several channels, but the source population is still unclear, whereas the clock comparisons are a closed loop between independent instruments. I would rather see B008 mature and its credit question settled than adopt it with one name now.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B009) first, arguing it is clean, reproduced by many laboratories, the basis of most superconducting processors, and not made premature by the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I ranked B009 third and agree with the science and its maturity. My qualification is a prize-allocation one. Girvin is among the 2004 proposal authors and not in the credited names, so the fair credit split cannot be supported from the supplied names. A second superconducting-circuit prize one year after 2025 also invites the question of whether the committee has covered that platform. I would rather not set that aside entirely, but I do not put it ahead of B006.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a metrology instrument as a discovery in the sense of the prize, or wait for the redefinition of the second to strengthen the impact case.

Priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel lattice-clock work (for example by Ye, Takamoto and others around 2003 to 2005), which I have not been able to verify independently from the supplied material.
Whether the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the trapped-ion clock community make a lattice-clock prize look derivative.

For B013, how to allocate between Mele and Hasan under the three-person limit, given that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is outside the credited names. This is the reason I stay with the cleaner B006 for now.
statement.conflict_note: No specific recusal issue is apparent for B006 from my profile. My mentor Sune Svanberg and PhD-period host John Hall are in the broader precision-spectroscopy tradition, but neither is a candidate here. I note an institutional overlap with Goran Johansson through the Chalmers-led WACQT, relevant to B009 (circuit QED) but not to my preferred configuration, and my own rare-earth quantum-memory work and company interests are not connected to any shortlisted candidate.
